2.text: camps of the neighborhood on the same day. Rich reindeer-breeders at their

3.text: slaughtering have guests gathered from far and near, including even members

4.text: of foreign tribes, such as Lamut, Eskimo, or Russianized Yukaghir.

5.text: The invitations are sent out beforehand; and if the guests live far away,

6.text: the host sends some one to bring them, so that there may be no excuse for

7.text: their missing the feast. It is customary for the host, if possible, to “wrap”
7.note: closing quote keyed curly (U+201D) per §1/§5.6; machine draft carried a straight quote here.

8.text: all the guests; that is, to make them presents of fawn-skins, killing a fawn

9.text: for each. If any distinction is made, a female guest takes precedence over

10.text: a male, and a stranger over a relative. Usually one fawn-skin is given to

11.text: each guest, while the first-comer gets two or three skins. Any other guest

12.text: who is bold enough to ask may also get more. To refuse such a demand

13.text: is dangerous, because the guest might take offence, and bewitch the host.

14.text: It is considered improper to make a present of meat, and keep the skin for

15.text: one’s own use. One who receives such a gift resents it, and may declare

16.text: aloud that the fawn does not walk without the skin. On the contrary, it is

17.text: quite proper to keep the larger part of the meat, and to give only the skin.

18.text: The number of fawns slaughtered at this ceremonial by a well-to-do

19.text: reindeer-breeder ranges from about a hundred to a hundred and twenty. At

20.text: least one third of these are distributed among the guests, while the remaining

21.text: two thirds are evenly divided; one half being destined for household uses, the

22.text: other for trade. Guests are not supposed to give return-presents. The poor

23.text: fellow-tribesmen, in truth, give none; but the neighbors afterwards present the

24.text: host with similar gifts. The visitors from foreign tribes usually return the

25.text: compliment later by giving some of their products. The Maritime Chukchee

26.text: and the Eskimo, for example, bring their former host a little oil or a coil of

27.text: thong; the Lamut give flint, and tinder made of fungus; the Russianized

28.text: Yukaghir, dried fish or a quarter of a cake of compressed tea. The host

29.text: has no right to grumble, should they bring little or nothing at all.

30.text: The ceremonial is accompanied by a foot-race, in which, in most cases,

31.text: only the young people or children take part. The prize is furnished by the

32.text: host. Wrestling-matches occasionally take place, but in these also only young

33.text: people participate. Shamans gather from the neighborhood and assist in

34.text: beating the drum. The occasion becomes quite a shamanistic contest when

35.text: the slaughtering is combined, as is usual, with the thanksgiving ceremony.

36.text: The latter is very important among the Chukchee, and will be described later

38.text: The guests go home the same evening, after the ceremony is ended.

39.text: The next day the dams whose fawns were slaughtered are milked by sucking,

40.text: thus adding to the daily fare of the family for several meals.¹ On the third
